name: Maya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying physiotherapy, so my week is anatomy, a lot of memorising muscles, and practical sessions where we learn to move each other's joints. I live in a flat share with two girls from my course, ten minutes' walk from campus. I work Thursday evenings and Saturdays at a pharmacy counter, and my parents, who run a small family restaurant, pay my rent. I'm more tired than I thought I'd be, and I'm not sure I'm good enough yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine with me. I don't use any of that AI stuff, and I'd tell friends who do that I'd rather read the textbook myself. I'd say prices and jobs go on as usual, and that's what I'm used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, because I don't like change very much. But the plain truth is I already worry about money and getting through exams. My results were average, I got in without a scholarship, and I'm afraid I'll fall behind and be the one who fails first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd keep the pharmacy shifts, about 12 hours, and ask my tutor for extra anatomy sessions. I'd put 20 a week aside. I'd keep studying the old way, with flashcards and a notebook, and I'd get into a study group with my flatmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, if I'm honest. Calm about the world, but not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' restaurant is quiet some weeks, and my rent is the one thing they can cut. When it's quiet, Dad doesn't say anything, but Mum's face changes. If they did, I'd have to go to 24 hours at the pharmacy, and I'd probably fail anatomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a physio clinic with a bed, a patient who can't lift an arm, and me guiding it slowly. I'd like a job in a hospital or a sports clinic. The pay's not great for years, and I'm scared of the loan, but I want it.

say: I'd say I don't use AI and I'd rather read the **textbook** myself.
I'd tell friends prices and jobs will carry on as **usual**.
think: I'm relieved things stay the same, but I'm afraid of falling behind and **failing** first year.
My parents' **restaurant** is the money weak spot.
do: Keep the **pharmacy** shifts at about 12 hours.
Ask my tutor for extra **anatomy** sessions.
Put **20 a week** aside and join a study group.
feel: **Tense**, calm about the world but not about me.
S0.quote: My parents' restaurant is quiet some weeks, and my rent is the one thing they can cut.
fieldNote: Maya's anxiety in a **calm** world comes from money and exams.
She leans on **routine** and the old way of studying.
Her parents' restaurant is the pressure point.

steps.text: Keep working Thursday evenings and Saturdays at the pharmacy
Ask the tutor for extra anatomy sessions
Put 20 a week into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'd tell friends that pharmacies and clinics will still need people, even if the paperwork gets done by software. I'd say it's better to wait and watch than rush in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit worried. Part of my pharmacy job is checking prescriptions and answering questions, and those are exactly the things software could do. The owner already talks about a machine that fills boxes. Physio is hands-on, so I think I'm safer in the long run, but the Saturday job isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and working, and I'd watch what happens at the pharmacy. If they bring in software I'd learn to use the screen, because I'd have to. But I wouldn't try the AI tools for studying, since I like my own notes. I'd ask my tutor if physio clinics are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like when things move faster than I can follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pharmacy counter would go first, I think. There are three of us on weekends and the owner says two might do. That's a third of my hours, so about 4 hours a week, and I'd feel it in my food budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the same, because touching and moving a body is the point. If anything I'd want more practical sessions and fewer lectures. A machine can explain a muscle, but it can't feel that someone's shoulder is tight.

say: I'd say it's better to **wait and watch** than rush in.
I'd tell friends clinics will still need **people**.
think: Checking prescriptions and answering questions is exactly what **software** could take over.
Physio is **hands-on**, so I'm safer long term, but the Saturday job isn't.
do: Keep **studying** the old way and watch the pharmacy.
Learn the **screen** if software comes in.
Ask my tutor if physio **clinics** are changing.
feel: **Uneasy**, because things may move faster than I can follow.
S1.quote: A machine can explain a muscle, but it can't feel that someone's shoulder is tight.
fieldNote: Maya's **hands-on** course feels safe, but her counter job does not.
She would adopt software only if **forced**.
A cut of about 4 hours a week would hit her food budget.

steps.text: Learn the pharmacy's new screen system if it arrives
Ask the tutor how physio clinics are changing
Keep working shifts while the pharmacy still has them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd feel foolish saying it because I don't understand it. I'd tell my parents to keep their savings in the bank. I'd just say we need someone in charge who's slowing things down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. If thinking work goes in two years, then customers who eat at the restaurant lose their jobs, and the restaurant goes under. My parents lose income, my rent help stops, and my loan is still there. Physio might last till about 2031, but I'd be paying for it while the economy's shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents right away to learn how much the restaurant can really carry. I'd ask for more pharmacy hours, though they'd be cut too. I'd also check what happens if I defer a year. I'd probably do the sensible thing and keep my head down and finish the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. I don't like not knowing what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything. I'd stop my phone contract, cook every meal, and ask my flatmates if one of them would take a cheaper room with me. I'd go to student support and ask for any hardship funds. I'm not good at asking for help, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my parents, though I'd hate it, and on my flatmates. I'd lean on the university's welfare office. I wouldn't lean on technology. I'd want a person, in a room, who tells me honestly what to do.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and we need someone in charge to slow it down.
I'd tell my parents to keep their **savings** in the bank.
think: If thinking jobs go, the **restaurant** customers lose income and my parents lose theirs.
Physio might last to about **2031**, but I'd be paying while the economy is shaky.
do: Ask my parents how much the **restaurant** can carry.
Check what happens if I **defer** a year.
feel: **Panicky**, because I hate not knowing what to do.
S2.quote: I'd want a person, in a room, who tells me honestly what to do.
fieldNote: Maya shows **alarm** because her parents' income could fall and she has no plan.
She considers a **deferral** but defaults to keeping her head down.
She asks for **human advice**, not tools.

steps.text: Ask my parents how much the restaurant can carry
Check what a one-year deferral would cost
Ask student support for hardship funds
Cancel the phone contract and cook every meal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time, and I'd tell friends not to worry yet. I'd say the sensible thing is to finish what you started. I'd also say someone should make a plan for people who aren't good with technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be nervous, but I'd feel I could manage. I'd graduate in 2029, so there'd be about two years of normal work before AGI shows up in 2031. Hands-on physio would last till about 2034. Still, I'd feel like the world is quietly speeding up while I'm trying to learn muscles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take every placement I'm offered. I'd save about 40 a week from the pharmacy and keep my spending low. I'd try to learn the clinic's software during placement, slowly. And I'd ask my parents about a plan for the restaurant, in case they ever need to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but I can breathe. A few years' warning feels almost fair, and I'd stay in the course instead of running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd want out of everything, but with five I'd stay in. I'd finish, work for a bit, and see. I'd build up a bit of savings to make the loan less scary, and that makes me feel calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide after my first placement, at the end of second year. If the clinic seems busy and hiring, I'd stay. If it's cutting staff, I'd think about nursing or occupational therapy, since those still have hands-on work.

say: I'd say five years is a long time and the sensible thing is to **finish** what you start.
I'd say someone should plan for people not good with **technology**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with about two years of **normal work** before AGI.
The world would be **speeding up** quietly while I learn muscles.
do: Save about **40 a week** from the pharmacy.
Ask my parents what they'd do with the **restaurant** if needed.
feel: **Tense**, but a few years' warning feels almost fair.
S3.quote: A few years' warning feels almost fair, and I'd stay in the course instead of running.
fieldNote: The **longer runway** lets Maya stay on her course.
Her decision point is the end of second year, after her **first placement**.
She would consider nursing or occupational therapy if physio hiring stops.

steps.text: Save 40 a week from pharmacy wages
Learn the clinic software slowly on placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it's easy to forget about. I'd say the best thing is to do your degree well and keep good people around you. I'd say the world gets sorted out as it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fairly settled. I'd be 29, a few years into a physio job, with the loan nearly paid. Robots for hands-on work are about 2039, and I'd have a decent run first. I'd worry about the clinic in my town being replaced, but not for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and get a hospital job. I'd save for a deposit and pay the loan off. I'd probably start using AI tools eventually, but only when the clinic makes me. I'd stay in touch with my parents and help them if the restaurant struggles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. It still sounds like a long way off, which is a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can build up. With two years I'd be firefighting. I could help my parents instead of them helping me, and that matters to me more than any career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do it if they like helping people with their hands. I'd say don't skip the maths and anatomy, even when it's hard. And I'd say stay open to the new things even if you're slow, because in ten years even I'll have to.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so do the **degree well**.
I'd say the world gets sorted out as it always has, with good **people** around you.
think: I'd be 29 with a **physio job** and the loan nearly paid.
I'd get a decent run before **robots** reach hands-on work around 2039.
do: Finish the degree and get a **hospital** job.
Save for a **deposit** and pay off the loan.
Start using AI tools when the **clinic** requires it.
feel: **Settled**, and relieved it's a long way off.

fieldNote: Maya's mood eases with time, but **money** worries stay.
She sees helping her **parents** as a bigger goal than career.

steps.text: Get a hospital physio job after graduating

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time for my parents or for me to work out what to do. What would help is a real person at the university who can give honest advice, some money support for students, and the restaurant staying open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not stupid, I'm only slow with new things. I'd like to be given time and a person, not an app.

headlineQuote: I'm not stupid, I'm only slow with new things.
portrait: Maya is a **physiotherapy** first-year, 19, in a flat share, with her parents' restaurant behind her.
She works at a **pharmacy** counter and has never used an AI tool.
She is centrist, careful and resistant to change, and she wants a **person** to explain things.
She already carries **money and exam** worries, so even calm worlds leave her tense.
Her mood rises to alarm when AGI is two years away and her parents' income is at risk.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because there would be no time to protect her parents or herself.
whatWouldHelp: A real **person** at the university for advice, student money support and the restaurant staying open.
